lines.text: On Nicomachus’ Introduction to Arithmetic

Translated from the Greek text of Ermenegildo Pistelli (Leipzig, 1894). The numbers in the margin are the section numbers of the digital (First1KGreek) edition of Pistelli’s text; they do not correspond to Pistelli’s pages, the standard reference for this work.

In beginning our particular account of the mathematical sciences, distinguished as they are part by part, we begin from arithmetic; for the study that belongs to it is by nature the elder, because it deals with simpler and more primary things, and for this reason the account of it also precedes the other mathematical sciences. Now this account too is not simple but of many forms; for as many as are the genera of beings, it is divided along with them all and admits the same divisions.

But before the numbers that are contemplated in other things one must contemplate number itself by itself, and starting from this we shall be able to examine also the number that is in nature, or in moral characters, or in the forms, or in general in all the things that are. For this reason, then, we must take up the mathematical science of numbers. For indeed this must be laid down first, as in the place of a foundation; for when it has been laid down beforehand it is possible for the other sciences also to be acquired, but without it those too are not acquired. And with a view to learning, too, one must begin from here; for once the necessary theorems in the mathematical sciences have been determined beforehand, we are guided through them to the more perfect studies of numbers; for it is clear that those are in harmony with this one. As for the conception of it, it is right to set it before us not as consisting in bare notions, nor as arising subsequently upon sensible things, nor as stripping off and separating certain images from sensible things, but as able to fit common concepts to all numbers, in whatever way they subsist. It is about mathematical arithmetic of this kind, then, that we now propose to speak.

Now we find that Nicomachus, in his Art of Arithmetic, has set forth everything concerning it in accordance with the mind of Pythagoras. For the man is great in the mathematical sciences and had as his guides in them those most experienced in mathematics; and, apart from this, he hands down with precision a wonderful order and theory and, together with wonderful demonstration, a knowledge of the scientific principles; he knows how to give an account of them, and he hands down the theorems pure and genuine, in no way muddied by alien opinions. Further, he is varied and copious, orderly and articulate in his knowledge of numbers, and universality of knowledge and inventiveness are present in him in great abundance; for he hunts out the first constitution and the first generation of numbers. He has also the quality of leaving nothing out; for he has gone over all the genera and species of numbers in common, has comprehended infinite things in finite ones and disordered things in ordered ones, proceeds through genera and species in order without passing over what comes next, and comprises in a single complete theorem what is circulated incompletely in many theorems.

Here he has also what one would least find present in him in his other books, conciseness and precision, and together with these fullness and completeness, a manner terse and compact, rich in thought and fertile—because, as I for my part believe, he sets down the Pythagorean mathematical doctrines on number themselves in their purity; but let anyone who wishes conjecture about this as he wishes. What must be concluded from all this, however, is the following. For if on all these grounds we prefer this man as the most skilled of all in arithmetic, it is with good reason that we for this cause set down his whole Art of Arithmetic, thinking that we ought neither to publish it incompletely, having lopped off its leading parts, nor to rewrite it—for this too would be superfluous—nor to appropriate what has been written; for it is an act of the utmost ingratitude to rob the author of the reputation that falls to him. Nor yet, on this account, ought we to compose discourses foreign to the Pythagorean schools; for it is not our purpose to say new things, but the doctrines held by the men of old, and hence, neither taking anything away nor adding anything, we now set out in our discourse the Art of Nicomachus itself.

But in order that the present treatise may not be incomplete in this respect either: Pythagoras was the first to give philosophy its name, and he said that it is a desire for and, as it were, a love of wisdom, and that wisdom is knowledge of the truth in the things that are. By ‘things that are’ he understood and meant the immaterial, eternal and alone active things, that is, the incorporeals; while the rest are ‘things that are’ only homonymously, so called by participation in these—corporeal and material forms, subject to generation and destruction, and never truly being. Wisdom, he said, is knowledge of the things that are in the proper sense, and not of those that are so homonymously, since corporeal things are not even objects of knowledge and do not admit of secure cognition, being unlimited, not to be comprehended by science, as it were non-existent in contradistinction to the universals, and unable even to fall under a definition with any clear circumscription. But of things that are by nature not knowable it is not possible even to conceive a science; it is therefore not likely that there is desire for a science that does not subsist, but rather for the science concerned with the things that are in the proper sense, that always remain the same and in the same state, and that always coexist with their appellation. For indeed it happens that the apprehension of these is accompanied by that of the things that are homonymously, though the latter was never made an object of pursuit, just as knowledge of the particular accompanies knowledge of the universal; ‘for accordingly,’ says Archytas, ‘having discerned well concerning universals, they were bound to see well also concerning particulars, what they are like.’

Hence the things that are are neither of a single kind nor simple, but are at once seen to be varied and of many forms: both the intelligible and incorporeal things, whose appellation is ‘things that are’, and the corporeal things that have fallen under sense-perception, which by participation have a share in coming truly to be. It would follow that we should give a systematic account of absolutely all the things that are, in some such way as this. The whole nature of the continuous and of the discrete is conceived along with the things that are—that is, with the constitution of the entire cosmos—in two ways: that of the discrete by juxtaposition and heaping, that of the continuous by unification and mutual coherence. Properly speaking, the continuous and unified would be called magnitude, the juxtaposed and discrete, multitude. And in respect of the essence of magnitude, the cosmos would be conceived and spoken of as one, solid, spherical, grown together with itself, extended and cohering; while in respect of the form and notion of multitude, on the other hand, the arrangement and ordering and harmony of the universe would be conceived as having its constitution out of so many, let us say, elements and spheres and stars, genera and animals and plants, contrarieties and likenesses.

But of the unified, division is in every case to infinity, while increase is up to a definite limit; whereas of multitude, by a reciprocal relation, increase is to infinity, but division conversely is up to a definite limit—both thus being by nature, so far as conception goes, infinite, and for that reason not to be circumscribed by sciences; for ‘there will not be anything at all that is going to be known, if all things are unlimited’, according to Philolaus. But since it is necessary that the nature of science be discerned in things that have been so precisely fashioned by divine providence, certain sciences, cutting off a portion of each and setting a limit to what they had comprehended, called what was taken from multitude ‘quantity’, which is thereby knowable, and what was taken from magnitude, in the same way, ‘size’; and they brought both these genera under sciences, their own forms of knowledge—quantity under arithmetic, and size under geometry.

But since these were not of a single form, and each of them admitted a still more particular subdivision—for of quantity one kind was by itself, free from any relation to another, such as, for instance, even, odd, perfect, deficient and the like, and the other was in some way related to something else (which is specifically called relative quantity), such as equal, unequal, multiple, superparticular, superpartient and the like; and again of size one kind exists and is conceived as at rest, the other as in motion and revolution—for this reason, naturally, two other sciences joined the two already brought forward and took hold along with them of the study of each object of knowledge. For with arithmetic, which received as its own province the inquiry into quantity by itself, music came to share in the systematic treatment of relative quantity (for its harmonic part and its part concerning concords profess nothing other than to articulate the relations and ratios of the notes to one another and the quantity of their excesses and deficiencies); while to geometry, which is occupied with the examination of size that is at rest and stationary, spherics came as a helper, having been established as the judge of size in motion—of that size, namely, which is most perfect and has received an ordered and uniform motion.

Hence, since they are occupied with subjects that are sisters, it is reasonable to consider these sciences too as sisters, so that the saying of Archytas may not go unheeded, ‘for these mathematical sciences seem to be sisters’, and to regard them as holding on to one another in the manner of the links of a chain, and to hold that the kinship of these sciences ought to show itself as one, ending in a single bond, as the most divine Plato says, to him who learns in the proper manner; and the man who has grasped all these things in this way, as he himself lays down, him he calls most truly the wisest, and he strongly affirms it in play; and he enjoins upon those who are eager to philosophize that these sciences are to be pursued and chosen by all means, whether they be difficult or easy—and very reasonably so, if indeed apprehensions of the continuous and the discrete come about through these alone, and the cosmos and all things in it are composed of the continuous and the discrete.

Now the exact apprehension of quantity is wisdom, and philosophy is the striving after wisdom, and philosophy, alone of all the arts and sciences, secures for man the end that is proper to him and in accordance with nature, and leads to the happiness that belongs to him alone beyond the other animals and is pursued in accordance with nature, as the end most fit to be his aim. Of these four sciences, moreover, arithmetic plainly takes the lead, because it is found to be prior and more primordial. For it abolishes the rest along with itself, and again is implied along with them; and things that abolish others along with themselves but are not abolished along with them, or, put otherwise, that are implied along with others but do not themselves imply them, are shown to be in a way prior and elder. Hence the inquiry into the systematic treatment of arithmetic, as the very first, would be most reasonable and fitting.

Quantity—that is, number—Thales defined as a system of units (in accordance with the Egyptian view, since it was in Egypt that he pursued his studies); but the arithmetical one stands on its own, and so neither the unit nor the one will fall under these definitions.

Pythagoras defined it as the extension and actualization of the seminal principles in the monad, or, put differently, as that which subsisted before all things in the divine intellect, from which and out of which all things have been arranged together and abide, numbered out in an indissoluble order. Others of his followers defined it as a progression from the unit by the unit’s own magnitude. Eudoxus the Pythagorean said, ‘number is a definite multitude’, distinguishing species and genus, just as quantity was distinguished above. The acousmatics of the circle of Hippasus said that number is the first paradigm of the making of the cosmos, and again the discriminating instrument of the god who fashions the cosmos. Philolaus says that number is the sovereign and self-generated bond of the eternal continuance of the things in the cosmos.

The monad is the least of quantity, or the first and common part of quantity, or the principle of quantity; or, as Thymaridas has it, limiting quantity, since the beginning and the end of each thing are called a limit, and of some things the middle as well, as for instance of the circle and the sphere.

The more recent writers define it as that in virtue of which each of the things that are is called one; but this definition lacked the words ‘even if it be collective’. The followers of Chrysippus speak confusedly when they say ‘the monad is multitude one’; for it alone is set in contradistinction to multitude. Some of the Pythagoreans said ‘the monad is the boundary between number and parts’; for from it, as from a seed and an eternal root, the ratios increase in either direction reciprocally: those of the things that are cut to infinity growing smaller with an ever greater name, and those of the things that are increased to infinity, conversely, growing greater. Some defined the monad as the form of forms, on the ground that it contains potentially all the principles that are in number. For it is polygonal in the plane, from the triangle on to infinity, and solid, showing itself in all the forms, and spherical and conical, and recurrent, and a side and a diagonal, and, what is most general, heteromecic, whenever it potentially affords the notion of a greater arisen from itself, and proportional and relational according to the ten relations, and in various other ways, in as many as will be pointed out.
It is called monad (μονάς) from its abiding (ἐπιμένειν) throughout in its own principle; and so with all the other things too that are in this way given their principle by it.

Again, from another beginning: of quantity, by the first division, one part is even and the other odd. The even is that which is able to furnish from itself equal parts, both the greatest and the least: the greatest in size and in their relation to the whole, because it is divided into halves, and the least in quantity, because into two (for there are by nature no parts fewer than two, seeing that there is no number short of the dyad either; for this is the first system of units, which is the very definition of number in general); the odd is that which in every case, when it is divided into the fewest parts, yields parts unequal to one another. For it is not divisible in two into equal parts; for this would do away with the monad, which is by nature indivisible and which is of service for the whole systematic treatment and for inquiries into nature of this kind. And since the even number, in whatever way it is divided, whether into equal or into unequal parts, is in every case resolved into parts of the same kind, for both are either even or odd, whereas the odd is resolved into parts that differ, namely both the lengths of number, those of the school used to call the even ‘heteromecic’ from what thus befalls it, in accordance with the meaning of the word, as having in its partitions only the one of the lengths of number; and in contradistinction to this they called the odd ‘amphimecic’, as furnishing both of these together.

They may also be made known through one another in the natural series of number: the even is that which differs by a unit in either direction from an odd, and the odd that which differs by the same from an even. Each genus is given its form both properly and accidentally: the even properly by the dyad, and accidentally by the unit as well; for the unit runs through it always in dyadic fashion, whether unmixed or with a difference as well, whether pure or together with any number whatever of the same kind; the odd, on the contrary, is properly measured by the unit, when it is measured an odd number of times, and accidentally by the dyad, not however by the dyad in itself, but together with the unit. The monad, however, has as its special prerogative over all the odd numbers, as being that which gives them their form, that it is not divided even into unequal parts; and the dyad over the even numbers, that it is divided only into equal parts. Hence the Pythagoreans used to name the monad Atropos and Apollo and other such names, and the dyad, analogously, Isis and Artemis. And from the fact that the monad is by nature indivisible, the same monad will be seen to be a limit and a demarcation in either direction.

It is a limit for size, in order that from it, as from a whole, the division to infinity may begin; and for quantity, in order that in the same way the increase to infinity may be extended over against it, from it as a unit; and that from it as a whole there may arise a half, then a third, then a fourth, then a fifth, and so on, parts ever smaller and smaller, contrariwise to the increase of their names as it advances; while from it as a unit there arise a dyad, then a triad, then a tetrad, and so on in an advance without end, the increase following the names; and that from this there may spring up the generation of a manifold reciprocal denomination, the monad underlying both, size and quantity alike, in the manner of a joint, and making itself as it were a partition and boundary of their reciprocal denomination.

For if we take the monad, and draw from it, as from an angle, a figure in the shape of a lambda, and fill up one of its sides in order with the numbers continuous with the unit, as far as we please, for example 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and so on to any extent, and the other, beginning from the greatest of the parts, which is the half, the part nearest to the whole in magnitude, with parts that are likewise continuous in order, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/6, 1/7, and so on to any extent, we shall see the reciprocity of which we spoke, and a natural connection and well-ordered relation, such as the following.

Since the whole was divided into two, the part was named ‘half’ accordingly, and in this way the half was yoked with two; again, because it was divided into three, ‘third’, and into four, ‘fourth’, and so on in order as far as a hundredth and a thousandth and a ten-thousandth; and from this the necessity of division to infinity forces its way in, because it is extended alongside that which is admittedly capable of increase to infinity. And further, as twice one is two, so half-times one is a half; and as twice two is four, so half-times a half is a fourth; and as twice two twice, so half-times a half half-times: eight, and an eighth; and as twice three is six, so half-times a third is a sixth. And in general, whatever we take from either side, the ratio remains the same in it; and whatever holds without qualification in the case of each of the numbers will in every case be found, in proportion, in the case of the converse parts as well. But this must be grasped beforehand, as it will be useful for what follows: that, while all the parts answer in denomination to all the numbers, the half alone answers to two in fact, but not in name as well; for the language is wanting in this, as in many other things.

The generation of the odd is both from the unit and by an unbroken composition, not the cumulative kind but that by pairing, which some call ‘conjugate’: for example, first one, then 1 and 2, then again 2 and 3, and again 3 and 4, and so on in the same way. That of the even is by interweaving, as 1 and 3, 2 and 4, 3 and 5, 4 and 6, and so on to any extent, in order that the dyad, as that which gives the even its form and as its element, but not as actually even, may be left out; or, in another way, by each of the numbers from the unit being doubled, as twice one and twice two and, in order, twice three, twice four, by which the giving of form to the even by the dyad, stated above, is made clearer. They may also be generated from one another, in the following way, so as to exhibit the property of number: for each of the two is half of the numbers of the other kind on either side of it taken together. And the most wonderful thing, which is both peculiar to the monad and goes to establish that it is not yet a number, is that, being bounded on one side only and not on both, it is the half of the dyad alone, contenting itself with its one neighbour.

Thus all the forms both of even and of odd are seen potentially in it in common, as in a kind of source and undifferentiated root of both, and one that is of necessity indivisible, unlike all the others. For against those who force the monad to be divided, and who set beside it on the other side the half, as a single quantity, continuous and of the same kind, there stand in the way the fact that, while all the numbers above it are yoked by their derived names with the parts severally opposed to them, it is itself set over against the whole alone; and the fact that there will in any case be a confusion of the two generic forms of number if we should say that the odd too is cut; and again the fact that it is possible rather to set beside it, on the side of the less, the nothing instead of the half, which in many places, even against our will, plainly admits itself into the nature of the theory: here, in the fact that the monad too is half of those on either side of it taken together, the dyad and the nothing, just as each of the remaining numbers was seen to be half of those on either side of it taken together; and there, far more and more plainly, when, 9 being the very first odd square after that which is so potentially, there appears in its mean, that is, in five, the principle of justice, making requital pair by pair according to arithmetic proportion, and just as the Pythagoreans define it when they say that justice is a power of rendering what is equal and fitting, contained in the mean of an odd square number.

For when the numbers from the unit up to the ennead are set out in a row, five, being the middle one, will mark off those on the near side of itself as having less than is fitting, and those beyond it as having more than their share, and that progressively: for those that come nearer to the ennead have always more, and those nearer to the unit always less; and what is fitting for each, by the principle of equality at any rate, is the ninth part of forty-five, the sum of them all, which is at once manifest in the mean between the more and the less, and in it alone, since justice too and the other virtues are found to be means between these and nothing else. For this reason, by as much as 9 exceeds what is due and has more than its share, by so much the first falls short; and by as much as 8, by so much the second; and by as much as 7, by so much 3; and by as much as 6, by so much 4; for with the gradual approach to the middle, as toward the suspension-cord of the beam of a balance, an equalization comes about, just as there too there comes about a rightness of the angles, both of those which the scale-pans make with the beam and of those which the beam makes with the suspension-cord itself.

But the middle number, 5, falls short by as much as it exceeds: by nothing, therefore. And this is one indication that the nothing is useful in the theory, and another shows itself at once. For not only is it in accord with this that 5 (ε) is, even in the shape of its written character, the half of 9 (θ), but also, further, that on account of their kinship the products paired on either side of it have by nature the same ending: for nine times 9 ends as once 1 does, eight times eight as twice two, seven times seven as three times 3, six times six as four times 4, and five times five alone ends as itself.

Further, nine times 5 ends as once 5 does, nine times 6 as once 4, nine times 7 as once 3, and nine times eight as once two. And again eight times 7 ends as twice 3, and eight times 6 as twice 4, and eight times 5 as twice 5, and seven times 6 as three times 4, and seven times 5 as three times 5. And, in another way, six times 5 ends as four times 5, if not in name yet at least in force, just as we also showed that the half answers reciprocally in denomination to two in force, but not in name.

If, then, like just judges who render what is equal and due, we were to take from those that have more than their share and give back to those that have less, we shall not take at random from any chance number and give to any chance number, but according to the same proportion, using as gnomon and, as it were, as rule the one that has neither overreached nor been overreached, that is, the pentad; for this number alone justly possesses its own in full. From 9, then, we shall take the fifth number counted from it and give it to 1, and the one that has done the greatest wrong and the one that has suffered the greatest wrong will be made equal; and the fifth from 9 is 4, for there are 8, 7, 6, 5, 4. Again, from 8 we shall take away 3 and add it to 2; for the fifth from 8 is 3. And from 7 we shall take away the fifth from it, 2, and add it to 3, and they will be made equal.

And again, taking away from 6 the fifth from it, 1, we shall add it to 4, and they will be equal. But from 5 we shall take away nothing (for the fifth from it is nothing) and add it to 5 itself, and it will be equal to itself. Thus what is conceived as less than the monad, the monad being indivisible, namely nothing, everywhere preserves the proportion in relation to the monad, rather than the half, as those people supposed; and the monad too has itself turned out to be the half of the terms on either side of it added together, for the half of 2 and nothing is 1. Indeed the very name of nothing most expressively signifies to us that the monad is by nature least and indivisible; for “nothing” (οὐδέν), when divided as “not even one” (οὐδ’ ἕν), takes away all being, which would not be so conceived if there existed a half of the monad, or a third, or the like parts of it. For why need one weave in besides the fact that the monad, when it multiplies any number whatever, does not go beyond that very number, seeing that even when it does this to itself it does not depart from itself, as being by nature a boundary between number in the unqualified sense and nothing? For a number, whether it takes itself or another, brings the reckoning to rest in neither, but in every case begets some third number; whereas nothing, whether it should seem to multiply itself or something else, will never go beyond itself: for no times nothing, and no times 9, is nothing, since this is equivalent to “in no way 9”; and likewise in the other cases.

But the monad, as intermediate between the two, if it takes another number, leaves the reckoning in that number, and if it takes itself, in itself. And it must further be added, along with what has been shown besides, that advance answers reciprocally to descent and descent to advance. Thus once 9 is 9, and the reckoning has remained in the outermost extremes. And twice 9 is 18, and the reckoning has passed over to the second extremes; and so on in succession. For it belongs to another occasion to investigate further how, when the number is also arranged as a square from its exposition in a row, no fewer plausible results follow in addition, by nature and not by convention, as Philolaus says somewhere: the 5 being found here too, in like manner, to be the mean along the three rows taken now one way and now another, and only those that attend upon it in length and in breadth and also diagonally having received what is due to them, while those not so placed have more than their share or less, and that not at random, but according to a certain proportional reciprocity.
But for the present, referring the full account of these matters to the discussion specially devoted to justice, let us proceed to what comes next.

Of the even, then, by subdivision, one kind is even-times even, and another, its counterpart, even-times odd, these being as it were extremes; and intermediate between them and, so to speak, common to both is the odd-times even. Not knowing this, Euclid and his school confusedly suppose the same number to be both odd-times even and even-times odd, having observed nothing with precision in this topic, most elegant though it is, as will be shown in what follows.

An even-times even number, then, is one that has its halves, and the halves of its halves, and further those of the parts below these, always even, as far as the unit; and for this reason it is an attribute of it alone to be measured by an even number only an even number of times. But if any number is, in addition to this, also measured an odd number of times by an even number, it will escape the description and will belong to one or the other of the remaining species. So here too Euclid again defines erroneously when he says: ‘An even-times even number is one that is measured by an even number an even number of times’; for see, 24 is measured four times by 6, which is even, and six times by 4, and various others likewise, and yet they are not even-times even, not even on his own view; and a consequence of the even-times even is that both it and its parts and the parts of its parts admit resolution into two, and this as far as the unit, which is by nature indivisible. It seems to have obtained its name not only from being measured by an even number an even number of times, but also because every part that may be taken in it has an even name. And again the value contained in each part, that is, its units, is itself likewise even, in the same kind.

Its generation is the double ratio advancing in proportion from the unit to infinity. But if the even-times even numbers are set out from the root in an odd exposition, converging upon a single mean, the extremes among them will correspond reciprocally in name, and those next after them, and so on continuously as far as the terms beside the mean, so that the product of each pair is rendered equal to the square of the mean, since it alone, one and the same, answered to itself in name. But if they are set out in an even exposition, the relation will be divided between two means that correspond reciprocally in name to each other, so that their product too is rendered equal to the product of the terms on either side of them, in regular order continually as far as the extremes. And in the advance of their generation the greater will in every case have, as their difference from the lesser, the lesser themselves, so that as a result the differences too, and again the differences of the differences, and those of these as far as is possible, keeping its ratio, are arranged in the manner of a triangle. And by their cumulative summation there arises in every case a generation of odd numbers, which will be useful to us a little later for the generation of the perfect numbers.

For in it the term that is about to come is always shown in advance, short by a unit, and all the terms to come are generically even, since the exposition consists of such numbers. And every even number, short by a unit, is necessarily odd. And in all expositions in proportion it is confirmed that the unit remains by nature indivisible; for it alone yields the appellation of the whole, which on each occasion corresponds reciprocally in name to the greatest term.

The even-times odd is the number which is itself also divided into two equal parts, in accordance with what is common to the even, yet does not have its parts further divisible, but each of them immediately odd; whence it also got its name, because, being even, it has its greatest parts immediately odd, or rather because the values of the parts in it are at variance with their names, being even when those have odd names, and odd when they have even names. And it was said to be opposed to the first species of the even not in this respect only, but also because of this species the greater extreme alone is divisible, and only once, being indeterminate and different at different times, whereas of that the lesser alone is indivisible, being determinate and always the same.

It is generated when the dyad multiplies the odd numbers in their order, so that, since the gnomons differ from one another by a dyad and that which multiplies them is also a dyad, the difference between the successive products is a tetrad; for this is twice two. And if we begin from the potentially odd, the result is the potentially even-times odd, 2; but if from the actually odd, 3, the actually even-times odd, 6. In the natural exposition of number, then, such numbers will be given their form by the dyad, will pass over three, will differ by a tetrad, and will be fifth from one another. And since the continuous, which is size, was seen to be the reciprocal counterpart of the discrete, that is, of quantity, and the former species has already made use of the proportion proper to size, this species too will make use of that proper to quantity, as being the opposite of the former; and so in accordance with the arithmetic mean the extremes added together will be equal to the means in an even exposition, and in an odd one to the mean taken together with itself, that is, they will be double of it, just as in the even-times even the square answered geometrically to the rectangles, where it resulted that the extremes, and the terms next within them as far as the middle, when multiplied by one another become equal to the product of the mean multiplied by itself, or else to the two means, these too being multiplied together just like the extremes on either side of them, in an even exposition of course.
And a property of this species, contrary to that of the former, is that it is measured only either by an even number an odd number of times or, conversely, by an odd number an even number of times.

But since at this point there is a more conspicuous error in Euclid, namely his failure to distinguish the even-times odd from the odd-times even, and to recognize that one of them is opposed to the even-times even while the other is a mixture of both, let us speak still more clearly about the third, first setting out Euclid's own words concerning them. For he speaks thus: ‘An even-times odd number is one that is measured by an even number an odd number of times.’ And the same number is also odd-times even, for it is also measured by an odd number an even number of times, as, for example, 6: for if we say “twice three” it is even-times odd, and if “thrice two”, odd-times even; very naively.

But in the third of his arithmetical books too he confounds the three into one, being evidently a slave to the suggestion of the name; for he says: ‘If an even number has its half odd, it is both even-times odd and odd-times even’, evidently saying the same thing as before. Then he adds: ‘If an even number neither has its half odd nor is one of those doubled from the unit, the same number is even-times even and even-times odd and odd-times even.’ So much for Euclid; but let us rather describe the third species as that which is in common moulded out of both, receives its form from both, and possesses their attributes. It is, then, a blend of them in its definition as well: for it is measured by an even number an even number of times, and the same number is measured by an even number an odd number of times, whereas this belongs to neither of the former both at once, but only the one attribute to the one and the other to the other. Moreover, its being divided more than once it has from the even-times even, and its not descending as far as the unit from the even-times odd; and in that the names of its parts are at variance with their values it shares with the second, while in that they also at the same time agree in name it is not cut off from the former; and on the side of the greater extreme, because it is bisected more than once, it runs to join the species that is bisected as far as the unit itself, departing from the one that is halved only once, whereas, in having besides the lesser extreme other parts too that are not resolvable, it to that extent departs from the former and becomes close to its opposite.

Its generation too is a mixture from both. For one must set out all the gnomons of the even-times odd in succession from the triad, and the even-times even numbers themselves on their own account, these being gnomons as well, in order from the tetrad; and then, starting from whichever side one pleases, for it makes no difference, one must multiply the first exposition term by term from the beginning, as far as one wishes, by the first term of the other, then the same terms again by the second, and after that by the third, then again by the fourth, and so on to infinity. For if the gnomons of the other are multiplied by those of the number that is divisible once, there will arise first numbers differing from one another by an ogdoad, doubles of the even-times odd, odd-times even numbers in breadth, in regular order from terms in regular order. Then, from a fresh beginning, come the doubles of these same numbers, quadruples of the original ones, having a difference quadruple of theirs, but necessarily double in relation to those before them; and so on throughout in the same proportion, the length too thereby coming into view.

If, conversely, the gnomons of the even-times odd are multiplied by those of the even-times even, the same results will follow, but the length and the breadth will change places with one another, as though by exchange. In order, however, that it may be still more plainly apparent that Euclid was ignorant of these things, one must observe also, in the more extended expositions both in length and in breadth, that the attributes belonging to both of those kinds are present together in this one alone, as being a mixture of them; for it will employ the geometric proportion as the even-times even does, making the product of the extremes equal to the square of the mean or to the product of the means, according to the number of terms set out, and the arithmetic proportion, rendering the sum of the terms that enclose the mean or the means equal either to twice the one or to the two taken once. Thus in all respects this number is shown to belong in common to both and to be, as it were, their offspring, the species of the even that came before it being opposed to one another, since it neither differs altogether from either nor is altogether the same. We must therefore correct Euclid's definitions and say that the number which is measured by an even number only an odd number of times is even-times odd, whereas the one that never has only the one character but always, of necessity, both, which neither of those has, is odd-times even, the two being together in it, reasonably a blend of both, and standing apart from the one by participation in the other that remains.

Of the odd number, again, by subdivision, one kind is prime and incomposite and the other secondary and composite; and, in another way, one kind is prime in itself, which is thereby at once prime and incomposite relative to another as well, and the other is secondary in itself, which need not also be secondary relative to another; rather, of this latter itself one kind is prime relative to another, while the other will be secondary and composite relative to another as well.

A prime and incomposite number, then, is an odd number which is measured completely by the unit alone and not by any other part besides; and such a number will advance in one dimension only. For this reason some also call it ‘euthymetric’, and Thymaridas calls it ‘rectilinear’ as well; for it is without breadth in its exposition, being extended in one direction only. It is peculiar to it to have no part except only the one that bears its own name, the magnitude of which is of necessity a unit. It is called prime not only because its measure is the unit alone and no other number (and the unit is the very first thing and the element of number), but also because no number can be observed before it, none at least that is a system of units, of which it will itself be a multiple; rather, it will plainly offer itself as the first, for certain other numbers to become multiples of it. And it is called incomposite because it could not be resolved into numbers equal to one another, from which it is clear that it was not compounded out of such numbers either.

Secondary and composite is the number that has the characteristics opposite to those of the one just described: a part besides the one that bears its own name, either one or more, and in the same way a measure besides the unit, either one or more. Such a number, in addition to being measured out linearly in a straight line, will also be set out as a plane, either as a square, if it has one part besides the one that bears its own name, or as a parallelogram, if it has at all events two parts answering reciprocally to one another, owing to the difference of its sides. More parts might be found in either case in a multiple, when the exposition has been made an odd number of times as far as the original numbers. It is called secondary because it employs also some second measure, or even several, besides the unit, and because among multiples it is never ranked first but, correspondingly, after a prime or primes; and composite because it can also be resolved into equal numbers, from which it is evident that it was also compounded out of such numbers.

Starting afresh: of the secondary species, one kind is secondary and composite both in itself and relative to another, as 9 relative to 15 or 21, and the other is secondary in itself but prime relative to another, as 9 relative to 25 or 35. For these numbers, taken by themselves, employ other measures apart from the unit, but relative to one another they employ it alone. We must reject those who say that, conversely, there is a number which is prime and incomposite in itself but secondary and composite relative to another; for they are deceived through comparing the measure itself with the thing measured, and they do not see that the numbers must have a common measure other than the unit and other than both of themselves. If this befalls any number relative to another, that number, being secondary in itself as well, will also be secondary relative to another. But it is possible, on the contrary, for a number that is secondary in itself not to be so relative to another. If any two odd numbers are proposed for the determination of whether they are prime or secondary to one another and, if secondary, what their common measure is, we shall continually subtract in turn the lesser from the greater as many times as possible, and the remainder from the original lesser number, and so on always in the same way, until the process ends either in a unit or in some other number from which it is no longer possible to subtract; and this number would be the common measure of the original numbers, which will then be called secondary to one another, as 15 and 35; for their common measure is the pentad.
But the unit shows them to be prime to one another and incomposite, whenever the process ends in it; for of such numbers it alone is the common measure.

In order that we may know how to generate in order all the numbers that are secondary and composite both in themselves and relative to one another, together with their measures and the correspondingly named parts, however many there may be, one must know a method of the following kind, which, like a sieve, will retain such numbers within the reckoning and will separate off the rest, namely the prime and incomposite, as things cast out. Set out in a row, in good order and in succession, the odd numbers from the triad, to the greatest length you possibly can; and, attempting to measure with the first, you will be able to measure completely, among those that follow, the numbers that leave two between them, without limit; with the second, those that leave four between them; with the third, those that leave six, and with the fourth those that leave eight; and, in general, with each number, those that leave between them twice as many as its own place in the order.

From this it is evident that each will measure, in accordance with its own name, the numbers that stand at the distance named after it, as 3, passing over two, always measures the third numbers, and so on consistently. But the first will measure the number first measured after it three times, in accordance with its own magnitude; the one after that five times, in accordance with the magnitude of the next number; the one following that in accordance with the magnitude of the third; and so on in like manner throughout; while the second, taking over this function in its turn, will measure the fifth number from itself by the magnitude of the number before it, the fifth again from that one by its own magnitude, the next fifth again by the magnitude of the number after it, and so on without end; and similarly in the case of the rest. And the notion of the potentially odd, that is, of the unit, will show itself here too, whenever each of the numbers set out, on taking over the measuring and multiplying itself, makes a square, as 9 from three times three. In such numbers there is sameness, which derives from the monad, as in once 9; but since otherness derives from the dyad, it is reasonable that the numbers produced from different numbers multiplying one another will also have their sides different, answering to one another according to the magnitudes of the gnomons, and such a number will be called oblong.

For the sake of clarity: how many times they measure will appear from the exposition of the odd numbers from the triad onward without limit, and how many numbers they leave between from that of the even numbers from the dyad (this too is a token of the everlastingness and mutual affection of the two species of number, even if they seem to be contraries, as right is to left, and yet in the same way helpful to one another), or indeed from the doubling of the place of each, in which the measuring number is ranked. The numbers, then, that are marked by these measurings are plainly secondary and composite, and their common measure is the number that has come upon them; while those that are passed over, like what is cast out through a sieve, are prime and incomposite.

Here too Euclid falls into a most manifest error in supposing the dyad to be one of the prime and incomposite numbers, because it employs the unit alone as its measure, having forgotten that it belongs to the species of the even, though it is odd-like in order that it may hold potentially, in a seminal manner, the principles of the kindred even-times even and even-times odd numbers, just as the monad holds those of all numbers without qualification; whereas the prime and incomposite numbers were seen to belong, by subdivision, to the odd species alone, and not to the even as well. At any rate he could not produce another even number of this kind, not even if he strained himself, so far is the one species of number by nature free of such a thing, just as the remaining species is free of the subdivisions of the former, the even-times even, the even-times odd and the odd-times even. But the dyad itself also, being as it were elemental and seminal, does not clearly partake of these subdivisions, although for them it is the leader of this genus, just as, of course, in other cases too the principles do not partake of many things that necessarily belong to the compounds: as the attributes of a line are not observed in a point, nor those of an interval in a note, nor those of a proportion in a ratio, nor corporeal attributes in matter and form, and as the attributes of many other systems, both drugs and mixtures, go beyond those of their several elements.

Again, starting from the beginning: of the even number taken by itself and here too entirely freed from entanglement with the odd, one kind is superabundant and another deficient, these being contrary to one another, while common to them and, as it were, a mean is the so-called perfect, differing in some respect from both and again in some respect partaking of both. It is superabundant, then, when an even number yields all its own parts, when added together, greater than itself and exceeding it in quantity; for this is why it has been so named, as being something faulty in its members, over-membered and overreaching, ranked in the class, as it were, of doing wrong and of having something more than falls to its share, as if someone had too many fingers on one hand or on a foot. It is deficient when, likewise, an even number, compared with all its own parts added together, is found to be greater, and makes its parts less than itself, which is why it has been so named, being deprived of the parts that properly go to complete it, like someone who is overreached, in suffering wrong and not having received what is his own, as if someone were tongueless or one-handed.
An example of the former is 12 and its multiples without limit, and 18 and 20 and many others of the kind; of the second, 8 and 10 and 14 and the like.

Perfect is that which is observed as intermediate between these and which has its own parts, when added together, neither more, like the superabundant, nor fewer, like the deficient, but midway between the greater and the less, which is to say equal, as it were by a kind of justice and receipt of what is its own and proper to it. Such examples accord with the correct view that the virtues are certain moderations and means between excess and deficiency, and not extremes, as some have supposed them to be; and that evil is opposed to evil, and both together to a single good, while good is no longer opposed to good, but to two evils at once: as cowardice is opposed to rashness, the common character of which is unmanliness, and both together to courage; and knavery to stupidity, the common character of which is folly, and both together to prudence; and prodigality to avarice, the common character of which is illiberality, and both together to liberality; and bashfulness to shamelessness, the common character of which is want of modesty, and both together to modesty; and in the case of the remaining virtues and worthy dispositions the analogous thing will become apparent to us if we attend to it, just as in the case of the relation of the unequal too it will be shown that greaterness is opposed to lessness, the common character of which is inequality, and both together to equality.

On this account, then, the rarity of the perfect number, as of something good and not of evil, which is abundant, will furnish us, by a law of nature, with only one among the units, that is, within the decad, and only one among the tens, that is, before the passage into * * * among the hundreds, and only one among the thousands.

And likewise, as it may be, only one in the first rank of the myriads, and again one in the second, and so on to infinity. Examples of this are 6 and 28 and 496 and 8128, and those like them, which end alternately in a hexad and an ogdoad. The method of their generation, too, is one that establishes the mutual affection of the species of number and their everlastingness in concord. For one must heap up the numbers that proceed from the unit in double proportion, that is to say the even-times even, adding them always one at a time, and examine the sum at the addition of each number. If a prime and incomposite number should result from the summation, let us multiply the number that has resulted by the last term taken in the addition; for the number so produced will in every case be perfect. But if it is secondary and composite, let us pass it over and add on the next term in the proportion, to see whether the number that results is prime and incomposite; for if it is, it must be multiplied by the term that was last added, and in this way the perfect number that is next in order will come to light. And so on without end. Thus through the addition of the even-times even numbers the nature of the even is indicated, and through the generation of odd numbers out of them, and above all through the production of the prime and incomposite, that of the odd.

One ought not to be surprised if a variety of things is predicated of the same number, as, for instance, of this very number 6, that it is perfect, and the first even-times odd, and again the first heteromecic, and that it is moreover called marriage by the Pythagoreans, because in it first of all there comes about a union of male and female by blending; and indeed on the same ground they call the same number health, and also beauty, on account of the completeness and symmetry of the parts in it. But those have misunderstood who suppose that they also call the same number friendship, on account of the coming together and befriending in it of things that differ; for it is certain other numbers that they expressly call friendly numbers, in their assigning of the virtues and the worthy dispositions to the numbers, such as 284 and 220; for the parts of each of them are generative of one another, in accordance with the account of friendship, as Pythagoras declared; for when someone asked ‘What is a friend?’ he said ‘Another I’, which is shown in the case of these numbers.
But since we shall set out in its proper place what the Pythagoreans refer to this sort of study, which is a most flowery and elegant one, we must proceed to what comes next.

For it follows upon these matters to treat of quantity that is no longer in itself but now relative to something, not because the whole technical treatment of quantity in itself has reached its end (for how could it, when we have discussed neither the plane numbers, which are of every variety, nor the solids?), but because these numbers contribute most of all to the understanding of those. For indeed we shall not complete the account of these in one continuous course either, but, aiming at the ease that the order affords the beginner, we shall for the most part deal with them after those, having deferred in turn the exposition of the proportions. What, then, a little earlier appeared to bear upon the account of the virtues, in the distinguishing of the perfect numbers and their contraries, this same thing shows itself to us again at the very beginning of relative quantity.

For of numbers considered as standing in some way in relation to another, the two most generic relations are equality and inequality; and equality, like a kind of moderation and mean, is undivided, admitting neither slackening nor intensification, whereas inequality is at its first division split into two, into the greater and the less, just as in the case of the virtues too their opposite, vice, was distinguished into excess and deficiency. The greater is opposed to the less, and both together to the equal; and nothing could be equal without being equal to something, nor greater or less without being so than something, which is why they are with good reason relatives. But to the equal the same name answers in return, as befits a mean, which is shown also in certain other examples of the relative, in the case of brother and fellow-soldier and neighbour and age-mate and others like them; whereas with the unequal something similar holds as regards the genus, but no longer as regards its species: there the answering term comes under a different name, as in other cases, such as father and teacher and beloved and the like. Equal, then, is a quantity which, when examined against its counterpart, has nothing more and nothing less; unequal is one which, when likewise examined against its counterpart, is either greater or less; for in this pairing the measure will leave something over in the thing measured after the single measuring.

And the greater is that which, when measured by the other, is of such a nature as to leave after a single application some part of itself, of whatever amount, unmeasured; the less is that which, being the measure of its counterpart, cannot encompass the whole of it in a single application. By subdivision these two species of the unequal yield five relations each, and both together ten. For of the greater, one kind is the multiple, another the superparticular, another the superpartient, and the remaining two, when the multiple is mixed with each of the others, are the multiple superparticular and the multiple superpartient; and of the less, by reciprocity and with the prefix ‘sub’, one kind is the submultiple, another the subsuperparticular, another the subsuperpartient, and the remaining two, mixed as in the former species from the multiple and each of the others, are the submultiple superparticular and the submultiple superpartient. The prefix in the names equips us to recognise the former as antecedents, as being first in nature and in dignity, as will be shown, and the second, which sink beneath them, as consequents, possessing the contrary characteristics.

If anyone should say that equality is not a relation, on the ground that the terms in it are without interval and without difference, he must be reminded that a relation is something other than an interval. For observe: in any chance example of inequality the interval between two terms is the same even if they are reversed, and yet when they are reversed the ratio, that is, the relation, is in every case different; so that nothing prevents the terms in equality from having no difference, being without interval, and yet in every case having a relation; otherwise the equal will not be among the relatives, which is impossible.

The multiple, then, is the first species of the greater, when of two terms the one measures the other more than once, and completely. It will begin from twice, so that from this they may take their names, the measured term being called double and the measuring term subdouble and, synonymously, half, just as, indeed, the remaining genus itself is called both submultiple and, synonymously, simply part; and if it is three times, the greater is triple and the less subtriple and third, and so with the other species in succession.

We shall have a clear illustration of all the multiples in their regular order if, having set out the continuous series of number from the unit, we compare either with the unit itself those that come after it, each one in succession, or with the dyad that follows it those that come after that, skipping one, each likewise in succession, with the triad those that skip two, or with the tetrad those that skip three, and so on to infinity, the multiples advancing in step with the setting out of number to whatever length it is carried. And if we write down in parallel rows all the species of the multiple, beginning from the unit, setting out in addition the successive series of number and generating the multiple relation in depth in relation to it, we shall observe many other delightful consequences and a varied elegance, and in particular an orderly generation of the corresponding naming of superparticulars of every kind after multiples of every kind, according to their kinship, and of superpartients as well and, if one should look into it, of the mixed kinds too; and whole rows will be seen to stand to whole rows in one unvarying relation that advances in regular order, correspondingly both in breadth and in depth.

Moreover the roots of the superparticulars will be found in a single row in depth, the second from the root in the next, and the third and fourth according to their corresponding sequence with these, having as their differences the numbers in succession from the unit. And if we also remove the units along the breadth, as having nothing varied about them, and set in front in their place the continuous series of number under the same unit, we shall observe a certain elegance and, showing itself in seminal form, the principle of the method of the divinatory tablets, which is handed down among the epanthemata of the arithmetical introduction. And if the setting out of the multiples should be carried as far as the decad, there will be units at the corners both in length and in breadth, the extremes once and the middle one twice, so that here too the property of proportion is preserved; for the product of the extremes will be equal to the square on the mean, and one of the extreme units will have the role of a point, the other that of a square, and the middle one that of a side.

And whichever of the numbers in the diagram be taken, it will be half of the two on either side of it, both in length and in breadth. But if they are taken diagonally, in the one direction the middle term will be less than the half by a unit, and in the other greater by a unit. Moreover, from the corner at the beginning, that is, the unit, to the corner at the end, the diagonal will consist of squares alone, each flanked by two heteromecic numbers both in length and in breadth, so that here too that universal rule is preserved, that from two successive heteromecic numbers and twice the square that is the mean proportional between them a square is in every case generated, and conversely from two squares and twice the heteromecic number that is the mean proportional between them likewise a square, and in the one case odd squares, in the other even. Now the production of even squares occurs in the present case too, because it is the squares alone that are flanked, which are by nature alternately odd and even, and the heteromecic numbers that attend them are always even, and the middle term, whether it be even or odd, makes an even number when it is taken twice; but the production of odd squares no longer occurs, since the heteromecic numbers are not flanked by squares; for when the extremes are taken once, among which there is in every case an odd number, the oddness persists.

And at each square, on either side in the shape of a gamma, the relations are again observed in regular order from the beginning, that is, from the double. And if we should also flank the heteromecic numbers in the shape of a gamma with the squares, adding the extremes once and the middle term twice, we shall produce the odd squares which we said were here left out.

The diagonal numbers will have as their difference from one another, in the one direction, the odd numbers from the triad, from beginning to end, and in the other, the even numbers from the dyad, from the middle to the extremities, the well-ordered numbers on either side being paired with one another in equality.

A superparticular ratio arises, generically, when of the terms compared the greater contains the other and in addition one part of it; specifically, if the part is a half the ratio is sesquialter, if a third sesquitertian, if a fourth sesquiquartan, and so on in sequence always, the greater terms becoming antecedents in relation to the lesser, and conversely the lesser consequents in relation to the greater, these too always taking their name with the prefix ‘sub’. An example of them is had, for the sesquialter, if, when the continuous series of number has been set out, we pick out the even numbers from the dyad and compare with the first the number with none intervening, with the next the number with one intervening, with the third the number with two intervening, and with the fourth the number with three intervening, and so on in sequence.

For the sesquitertian it is had when we pick out the numbers from the triad that differ by a triad and compare with them, with the first the number with none intervening, with the second the number with one intervening, with the third the number with two intervening, with the fourth the number with three intervening, and so on in sequence as in the former case. We shall have an example of the sesquiquartan if we pick out the numbers from the tetrad that differ by a tetrad and again compare with them, with the first the number with none intervening, with the second the number with one intervening, and with the third the number with two intervening, and so always in the same way as in the cases already described. In the remaining species of the superparticular too we shall do what is analogous, taking, in accordance with the very name of the part, the first numbers that are able to furnish from themselves the part by virtue of which the numbers compared with them will be their superparticulars; and these latter will also differ from them by a unit and will become the roots of the ratios. The designation of the part, which is always considered with reference to the lesser term, will be greater in name by a unit with reference to the greater. But the examination of the part will not be made with reference to the greater terms, because none of the root terms will be found to possess that part by virtue of which each of them is the superparticular of the lesser term compared with it; and it is according to the roots that the ratios increase.

A superpartient relation exists when the greater term contains the lesser and in addition certain parts of it, more than one, obviously. If these are two, it is called superbipartient and the lesser term subsuperbipartient; if three, supertripartient and subsupertripartient; if four, superquadripartient and subsuperquadripartient, and so on in sequence. We shall have an example of superbipartients if, setting out the odd numbers from the triad, we compare with each of them the number with one intervening, and of supertripartients if, setting out the continuous numbers from the tetrad, we compare with them the numbers with two intervening. But since formations of this kind are not pure but are confused with other relations, we shall use the progressions according to the ratio of multiples, taking as roots, just as in the case of the single parts, the terms that will furnish from themselves the parts after which the superpartient is named: for example, of superbipartients, five to three, then the doubles and triples of these and so on to infinity; of supertripartients, seven to four, then the doubles and triples of these and so on in sequence; of superquadripartients, nine to five, and analogously throughout, so that the progression of the lesser terms in the roots goes by the successive numbers from the triad, and that of the greater terms by the odd numbers from the pentad.

In general we shall have the roots of every ratio as follows. In multiples, they are those in which the unit is the lesser term of the terms compared, and it is a special feature of the double that the same unit is also the difference. In superparticulars, in the sesquialter the dyad will be the lesser term, and the terms will again have a unit as their difference. In the sesquitertian and the sesquiquartan and the succeeding superparticular ratios the lesser term will be the one that furnishes from itself the name for the part by virtue of which the ratio is superparticular, and the difference in all of them will be the same unit.

But in the roots of the superpartient too the same unit, although it has no place either to show itself in the terms, as in the species of the multiple, or to be their difference, as in those of the superparticular, because the greater term exceeds the lesser by more parts than one, may be seen in the terms in another manner; for the parts left over unmeasured in the greater term, when compared with the lesser, will in every case have a unit as their difference.

It remains to speak of the mixed relations compounded of the multiple and the remaining two, the superparticular and the superpartient, and of the consequents of these, so that the relations of inequality too may have their generation naturally in accordance with the perfection of the decad, the antecedents being five, and five the consequents conjugate to them: the antecedents in the multiple, the superparticular, the superpartient, the multiple superparticular and the multiple superpartient, and the consequents, equal in number, named with the prefix ‘sub’. For the relation of equality, inasmuch as it has no difference but is as it were sameness and unity, since the equal is as one to one, will be of another nature, and indeed of the nature contrary to inequality, and for this reason will not be numbered together with the species of inequality.

Moreover, equality will have the role of a principle in relation to inequality, just as among linear things the right angle stands to the obtuse and the acute, and among musical intervals the mese to the notes that are tightened and slackened. For these too, taking their start from something definite and limited in accordance with the principle of equality, and from this having their deviation toward the greater and the less in accordance with inequality, proceed to infinity. In order, then, that it may be shown that the relations of inequality arise from equality by natural necessity and not by our own positing, first the multiple relation, beginning from the double, from which in turn comes the superparticular, taking its beginning from the sesquialter, and from this the superpartient in the analogous order, and next from these the mixed relations, one must set out three terms, first in units, then in dyads, and again in triads, and so on in sequence, and alongside each such setting-out one must fashion three other terms by means of three rules that are always the same, and alongside each set of terms so fashioned three more, and from these others again, and so on always in sequence.

At each formation one must try setting out the terms both in their natural order and in reverse, and, using the same rules, fashion as a second setting-out the terms derived from them. The rules will be these: make the first term equal to the first of those set out, the second equal to the first and the second together, and the third equal to the first, two seconds and the third together. From all sets of three terms, then, set out beforehand in equality, whether in units or in dyads or again in triads and so on, there will arise by the aforesaid rules generically multiples, and specifically, among multiples, the doubles: the first from units, the next in order from dyads, those after them from triads, and so on in sequence. From the doubles so fashioned come triples, the first again from the first and the next from the next; from the triples, quadruples, preserving their own good order; from the quadruples, quintuples; and always the succeeding ratios from those that precede. But if in fashioning them we do not use this setting-out of the terms in their natural order, but reverse the first terms fashioned from the equalities, so as to place the third term in the position of the first and the first in that of the third, while keeping the mean term likewise as mean, and then fashion others by the same rules, there will spring up generically superparticulars from multiples, and specifically sesquialters from doubles, well-ordered from well-ordered, sesquitertians from triples, preserving the same order, and likewise sesquiquartans from quadruples and sesquiquintans from quintuples and so on, the superparticulars that share the name of each species extending side by side with the species of the multiple by a certain natural kinship.

And from these same terms again, when they are reversed, we shall in every case generate the superpartient ratios, the first again from the first, the second from the second, the third from the third, and so on in sequence, these too being disposed in good order in correspondence with the original derivation of their names. For the sake of an example, let three units be set out beforehand in the ratio of equality. If, then, in accordance with the rules stated we make the first term equal to the first, it will be a unit; if the second equal to the first and the second, it will be a dyad; if the third equal to the first, two seconds and the third, it will be a tetrad; and the terms so fashioned will be in double ratio, 1, 2, 4.

From these, by the same rules, we shall have the terms in triple ratio, 1, 3, 9, and from these the next after them, in quadruple ratio, 1, 4, 16, and so on in sequence. If we set out dyads beforehand in equality, the next terms, being likewise in double ratio, will be 2, 4, 8; from these again the next, the triples 2, 6, 18; from which the next, the quadruples 2, 8, 32; and all the rest follow together. But if we reverse the first terms in double ratio, 1, 2, 4, we shall by the same rules produce the first terms that are in sesquialter proportion, 4, 6, 9, and from these in turn, when reversed, the terms that are likewise in superbipartient proportion, 9, 15, 25.

From this the kinship of the relations becomes plain. For if the double ratio was generated from equality, and we have learned that the half takes its name from two, it is with good reason that next, as akin to it, the sesquialter ratio was fashioned among the superparticulars, and from this in turn, among the superpartients, in accordance with its affinity with the dyad, the superbipartient. If the first terms are in triple ratio, sesquitertians will grow out of them and from these supertripartients; if they are quadruples, sesquiquartans and superquadripartients, and so always with those that follow, preserving the affinity of the derived name, roots coming from roots, seconds from seconds, thirds from thirds, and always in the same way. But let us not suppose that the roots of superparticulars in three terms will be the same as those that appear in two; for when a given ratio exists in two terms it is not possible for a third term also to be procured that preserves the same ratio to the mean term, because the greater term is not capable of furnishing the same part by virtue of which it is the superparticular of the first, so that the third term too might by that part preserve the ratio to it.

For every root of a superparticular ratio, having its terms differing by a unit, will not have them divisible in like manner; but if the lesser is divided into two, the greater is divided into three, and if the lesser into three, the greater into four, and always the greater will admit a division greater in name by a unit than that of the lesser, so that, since in any ratio whatever the part is examined with reference to the lesser term, which is consequent in relation to the greater, there will be no third term as antecedent having the greater as its consequent according to that part. But since the roots in three terms are not the same as those in two, the roots will show themselves in the proportional terms in another way, for they will turn out to be their differences. For instance, since 4, 6, 9 are proportional in sesquialter ratio, their differences will be the roots that contain the same ratio, 3 and 2; and again, 9, 12, 16 being in sesquitertian ratio, the differences of these will be the root terms, 4 to 3; and always in the same way the same thing will happen in all the species of the superparticulars; for those will be roots in three terms whose differences are the roots in two.

In the multiples, the proportional terms set out from the beginning will always have their lesser terms as roots in each ratio. The cause of this is the unit, which offers itself as consequent to all the ratios of the multiple. None the less the differences in the proportional terms will also contain the same ratio, even though they are not roots of the ratios, as they turned out to be in the case of the superparticulars. Only the proportional terms in the double ratio from the beginning will have this as a special privilege, that they also have as their differences the lesser terms, which are precisely the root terms. In the species of the superpartients, the terms containing the roots of the ratios will appear neither in the differences, as with the superparticulars, nor in the lesser terms, as with the multiples, but according to a certain other well-ordered proportion. For the terms that are proportional in the superbipartient ratio will contain the root terms in the half of their differences, the kinship of the half with the dyad, in virtue of which the ratio is superbipartient, showing itself here once again; those in the supertripartient ratio will contain them in the third of the differences, those in the superquadripartient in the fourth, and those in the superquintipartient in the fifth, and the like will hold always in succession, the natural affinity of the fractional part with the ratio being preserved.

For the ratios taken by themselves too have, in respect of the parts, a name that is less by a unit when they are compared with the fractional parts in which the excess of the greater term over the lesser consists: for the first ratio will be superbipartient of thirds, the second supertripartient of fourths, the third superquadripartient of fifths, and so on in like manner.

The mixed relations, compounded of the multiple and of each of the remaining two, the superparticular and the superpartient, are themselves also generated from those that precede them: the one in multiple superparticular ratio from the one in superparticular ratio, from which the one in superpartient ratio was also generated; for example, specifically, the double sesquialter springs from the relation in sesquialters, the terms no longer being set in reverse order but in their natural order, while we make use of the same three rules: for, there being a proportion in sesquialter ratio, 4, 6, 9, whose differences are the root terms, the double sesquialter will be formed in the terms 4, 10, 25. From the proportion in sesquitertian ratio, 9, 12, 16, whose differences again are the root terms, when we begin in the same way from the lesser term, there comes the double sesquitertian in the terms 9, 21, 49.

And from the proportion in sesquiquartan ratio, 16, 20, 25, whose differences are again the root terms, the double sesquiquartan is generated in the terms 16, 36, 81, and so on in like manner, the kinship being preserved here too between the fractional part that runs on after the multiple and the name of the superparticular ratio from which the mixed relation has its generation. For when the generating relation is sesquialter, the one generated is double sesquialter; when it is sesquitertian, double sesquitertian; and when it is sesquiquartan, double sesquiquartan; and so on in sequence. Again, the roots of these too will be found arranged in good order, no longer showing themselves immediately in the differences of the terms that are formed, as happened with the simple relations; rather, because the relations are mixed and the ratios have been increased, they will be seen to lie in fractional parts of the differences.
