Again, in the exposition of numbers in proportion the third terms are squares, the fourth cubes, and the seventh at once cubes and squares. Every cube, when multiplied by its own side, makes a square, which will be as many times the cube as the square on the cubic side is of the side itself; and this latter square will itself be the square side of the number produced from the cube and its side.

Again, as from two squares multiplying one another a square arose, so from two cubes there arises a cube, and from a cube taking itself a number that is at once cube and square. And among numbers in proportion, if the one after the unit is a cube, the rest too will be cubes; and when four numbers are in proportion, if the first is a cube, the fourth too will be a cube; or again, when a cube measures a cube, the side too will measure the side. And practically all the attributes of squares will be observed, analogously, in cubes as well. Leaving, then, the discovery of such properties to those who will pursue these refinements for themselves, we shall pass on to the topic of proportions.

Proportion, then, is the likeness and sameness of several ratios. What ratio in the sense that concerns proportion is, since the word is used in many senses, we made clear in what went before: it is the relation to one another of two homogeneous terms. ‘Homogeneous’ is added because it is proper to compare things that fall under the same genus, for example a mina with a talent, whose common genus is weight, and a line with a surface or a solid; for magnitude is common to them.

There are also some things compared in respect of power and in respect of bulk, and certain other genera. But how things that are not homogeneous stand to one another it is not possible to know, for example a cubit to a cotyle, or the white to a choenix. Quantity too is one genus, and number belongs to quantity, so that comparison will arise in the case of the ratios in number as well: they will have a certain ratio and a relation of a certain kind. If the terms are in equality, the ratio is that of equal to equal; for equality is without difference; but in inequality it is according to difference. And interval will not be the same thing as ratio: the ratio is twofold, because the unequal too is two and not one, and the interval will be the same but the ratio different; for of two to one and of one to two the interval is the same, but the ratio is double and half, so that ratio is something other than interval; for indeed in the case of several terms, while the ratio is often the same, the interval is different, as in 4, 6, 9. That the ratio of inequality is in ten genera, five of them antecedent ratios on the side of the greater and an equal number consequent ratios on the side of the less, and that all have their generation from equality, we learned earlier in the topic of relations.

There is also a ratio called by this very name, that ‘of number to number’, because it falls under none of the ten genera, as will be shown in the harmonics: the ratio of the leimma, in the terms 256 to 243. The ratios in numbers being, then, of some such kinds, proportion will be the taking together of several ratios in likeness, in three terms at the least; for a ratio is said to be conjoined when there is a common mean term having a ratio to each of the extremes; for it is the common term that joins the ratios. A ratio is said to be disjoined from a ratio when they have no common term. This occurs in four terms, which is why ‘the proportional’ is thought to differ from ‘proportion’; for the proportional occurs in disjoined terms as well, whereas proportion in the strict sense is assigned to those that have a common term.

Since proportion, then, arises in three terms, the first term must have to the second the ratio which the second has to the third, or conversely, which is also why it has been so named (ἀναλογία); for the terms are set out according to the same ratio (ἀνὰ τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον). Their differences too will be in the same ratio; and if there is ratio in equality also, it is clear that there is proportion as well. Of this the most elementary is that in units, so that there may be a proportional monad also, then that in dyads, and third that in triads, and so on in sequence; from these, in accordance with the three rules stated earlier, the proportions in inequality are generated in good order.

It must be understood beforehand that the ancients gave the name proportion in the strict sense to the geometric, though by now, more loosely, all the rest as well are so called, which generically are means. That the name was with good reason restricted to the geometric will be stated in the account of it. In ancient times there were only three means, in the days of Pythagoras and the mathematicians of his time: the arithmetic, the geometric, and the one third in order, which was once called subcontrary but was afterwards renamed harmonic by the circle of Archytas and Hippasus, because it manifestly embraced the ratios that belong to what is attuned and melodious.

It was formerly called subcontrary because it underwent something subcontrary to the arithmetic, as will be shown. When the name had been changed, the later mathematicians of the circle of Eudoxus, having discovered three further means, called the fourth subcontrary in a special sense, because it too undergoes something subcontrary to the harmonic, as will be shown; the remaining two they named simply from their order, fifth and sixth. The ancients and those who came after them thought it possible to construct just so many means, that is, six; but the more recent writers discovered four others besides, contriving their generation out of the terms and the intervals.

The first, then, is the arithmetic mean, when the mean term has an equal interval to the extremes on either side, and exceeds and is exceeded by an equal number, but has different ratios to the extremes, the greater ratio being that to the lesser term and the lesser that to the greater, and these ratios being continuous though of different genera.

As an example of it: when the series of successive numbers from the unit is set out and any three terms whatever are taken, whether consecutive, or skipping one, or skipping two or three or four or as many as one wishes, the mean term in each selection exceeds the lesser and is exceeded by the greater by an equal number, for example 1, 2, 3 and 1, 3, 5 and 2, 4, 6. It is generated from equality in this way: a first term equal to the first, a second equal to the first and second, a third equal to the first and second and third; or again, a first from the first and second, a second from the first and two seconds, a third from the first, two seconds and the third. But from the equality in units, by the former procedure, there is generated the mean that has its terms with none omitted; from that in dyads, the one skipping one; from that in triads, the one skipping two; and in tetrads, the one skipping three, and so on analogously.

And if the first ratio is double, the second is in every case sesquialter, and that of the extremes triple. If it is triple, the second is superbipartient of thirds, and that of the extremes quintuple. And if it is quadruple, the second is supertripartient of fourths, and that of the extremes septuple, and so on analogously. It is a property of this mean that the mean term is the subdouble of the two extremes together. And again, as each term is to itself, so also is the excess to the excess; and this is the same as the terms being at an equal excess. The combinations taken from the unit by three terms will produce the polygonal numbers that are second in actuality, all exceeding one another by a triad; for from 1, 2, 3 there arises the second triangular number in actuality, 6; from 1, 3, 5 the second square in actuality, 9; from 3, 4, 5 the second pentagonal in actuality, 12; and so on in sequence. But if the terms are selected from the unit skipping one each time, the triangular number will no longer begin the polygonals, but the lead will pass over to the square; for the first will be 9, from the combination 1, 3, 5, and those that arise next will observe a certain principle that is not without order.

If the selection is made with an omission of two, so as to be 1, 4, 7, the pentagonal number 12 will begin. If with an omission of three, there will be from 1, 5, 9 the hexagonal number 15, and so on without limit, in conformity with the generation of the polygonal numbers themselves. For because the triangular numbers were produced from the numbers with none skipped, in the first constitution it is the triangular number 6 that will begin the polygonals; and because the squares were produced from the numbers skipping one, in the second constitution the square 9 takes the lead; and further the pentagonals from those skipping two; and this will hold throughout in sequence. Now since the first combination from the unit with none skipped is productive of a hexad, this first combination, 1, 2, 3, will give their form to those that follow it, when no term is taken in common nor yet any passed over, but after 1, 2, 3 there is taken 4, 5, 6, then 7, 8, 9, and so on in sequence; for all these will turn out to be hexads, the decad always taking over the place of a unit, that is, being reduced to a unit; for it is in this way, as we were saying, that it is called by the Pythagoreans a unit of the second course, and the hundred a unit of the third course, and the thousand a unit of the fourth course.

For 4, 5, 6 makes the number 15; and when the decad is reduced to a unit, the five, taking this in addition, becomes a hexad. Again, 7, 8, 9 added together makes the number 24; reducing its 20 to two units I add them to the 4, and again I have a hexad. Again, adding together 10, 11, 12 I make 33, of which the 30 is a triad; adding this to the three I likewise have a hexad, and this will be so in the same way throughout. And the first hexad has no transposition of a decad into a unit, inasmuch as it is the form-giver and element of those after it; but the second will have a transposition of one unit, the third of two, the fourth of three, the fifth of four, and so on in sequence. And as many as are the decads transposed, so many enneads also will be subtracted from the whole sum, so that what is left may likewise be a hexad; for since 15 has a transposition of one decad, if I take away one ennead, a hexad will be left. And since 24 has two decads that are converted, if I take away two enneads, again a hexad will be left, and this will turn out so throughout.

One might find still more elegant properties attending the arithmetic mean, which we deliberately pass over for the present, having regard to the due measure proper to an introduction. This is the mean that Plato described as ‘exceeded by an equal amount in number, and exceeding by an equal amount’.

The second mean, the geometric, is called proportion in the proper sense, because its terms contain the same ratio, being separated according to the same ratio; for whatever ratio the terms have to one another, whether from the lesser to the greater through the common term or the reverse, this the difference also has to the difference; and the reason is that the terms will not be separated by an equal difference, as in the former mean. It is also possible for the proportional to occur in four terms, the ratios being disjoined. And, so that we may fit Plato’s saying to the proportion here, we must quote it: ‘For whenever, of three numbers, whether bulks or powers, the middle one has something in common, so that what the first is to it, that it is itself to the last, and again conversely, what the last is to the middle, the middle is to the first, then, the middle becoming first and last, and the last and the first in turn both becoming middles, it will follow that these are thus of necessity the same.’

Before Plato, too, Pythagoreans had made the same determinations about it. Thus Timaeus the Locrian, in his On the Nature of the Cosmos and the Soul (from which, they say, Plato furnished himself and composed the Timaeus that for this reason bears his name; among those who say so is Timon, the author of the Silloi, who speaks as follows: ‘For much silver he got in exchange a little book, and setting out from there he tried his hand at Timaeus-writing’), says something like this: ‘For of any three terms whatever, whenever the intervals too stand in the same ratio to one another, then indeed we see that the middle, by the measure of justice, is to the first just what the third is to it, and conversely and alternately.’ Geometric proportion belongs to continuous quantity, that is, to size, being separated according to equal and similar ratios; whereas the arithmetic belongs to discrete quantity, being separated no longer by equal ratios but by equal numbers in its excesses. And in the latter the ratios are different but the intervals the same; in the geometric, conversely, the ratios are the same but the differences different.

This mean too is generated from equality, by the same three rules that were used in the case of the relations; for all the sets of three terms there are in proportion according to this mean, standing thus: as the greater is to the mean, so is the mean to the lesser, and so is the excess of the greater over the mean to that of the mean over the lesser. It is a property of it to make the product of the extremes equal to the square of the mean term, if the terms are three or in general odd in number; but if they are four or in general even, it will make the product of the extremes equal to the product of the means. And in this mean the terms lengthen one another by blending, but in the arithmetic by composition, because such is the nature of discrete quantity and multitude, with which, again, arithmetic is properly concerned, as we said at the beginning of the introduction. Now among multiples, in proportional series of every kind, we shall find a great many examples of it, but among superparticulars and superpartients ever rarer ones, in step with the advance of the name of the part.

The reason is plain: every number is capable of being multiplied, but not every number can admit all parts; rather, those that skip one admit halves, those that skip two thirds, those that skip three fourths, those that skip four fifths, and so on, the numbers that have parts of greater denomination being ever more sparse. And if the ratios will be ever fewer because of the rarity of the numbers that will admit the part by virtue of which they will become superparticular or superpartient, much more will the proportions become rarer because of the addition of the third term; for a number that contains, besides the mean term, let us say, a half of it as well, does not in every case itself have a half, nor does one that contains some number together with its third part itself also have a third, and similarly with the parts that follow. But in order that a proportion may arise, it is necessary that the root terms which contain the ratios multiply one another, and these same terms will also show themselves in the differences of the proportion. And so that we may take a common example of root proportions in all the species of the superparticular, beginning from the sesquialter, and in addition in the first of the multiples, that is, the double, we must here too set out in rows the numbers that are same and those that are other, each kind from its own beginning, and fit them together by interweaving, so that each combination is of three terms, and in continuity, the last term of the preceding combination always beginning the one after it; for by this undisjoined selection each set of three terms from the unit will exhibit what is sought.

The third mean, the one called harmonic, exists when, of three unequal terms, as the greater term is to the least, so is the excess of the greater terms to the excess of the lesser, that is, the excess of the greater over the mean to that of the mean over the lesser. This mean differs from those before it in that the mean term neither exceeds and is exceeded by the extremes by an equal number, nor stands in the same ratio to them. Its roots are 2, 3, 6 or 3, 4, 6; for by the multiplication of these, or by their superparticular increase, if indeed they admit of it, many others will spring up. Some call this mean stationary, because it appears only in the aforesaid root terms, as being stationary and prototypical; for in the case of the arithmetic and the geometric it is possible to arrange an unlimited number of combinations.

At any rate, in both the root means the extremes are in double and in triple ratio to one another, and so are the differences of the greater terms from the means to those of the means from the lesser. The mean is called harmonic because the ratios found in harmony can be seen in it in seminal form: thus in 3, 4, 6 the concord called the fourth, which is the least of the concordant intervals, being observed in sesquitertian ratio, is in the lesser terms, that is, in 4 to 3; the fifth, which comes next after the fourth, being in sesquialter ratio, is in the greater terms, that is, in 6 to 4; and the octave, being composed of both the aforesaid and observed in double ratio, is in the extremes, that is, in 6 to 3. Moreover, the difference of 6 from 4 to that of 4 from 3 is likewise in double ratio, in accordance with the concord of the octave.

Furthermore, the power of the extremes multiplied into one another, 18, in relation to that of the mean multiplied into itself, 16, being in sesquioctave ratio, contains the interval of a tone; for in the prototypical terms 3, 4, 6 it was not possible for the ratio of this interval to appear, because none of them is able to furnish an eighth part, by virtue of which some other number would be its sesquioctave. Again, the power of the greatest is triple, and the triple ratio contains the concord of the octave and fifth together; and the power of the greatest by itself to the power of the least will have quadruple ratio, which contains the concord of the double octave. And again, starting afresh: the power of the least into the mean is 12, of the same into the greatest 18, and of the mean into the greatest 24; while the power of each on its own is, of 3 by itself 9, of 4 16, and of 6 36. And in sesquitertian ratio, the one that contains the fourth, are 24 to 18 and 12 to 9; in sesquialter, that of the fifth, are 18 to 12 and 24 to 16 and 36 to 24; in triple ratio, so that the octave and fifth may be constituted, 36 to 12; in quadruple, so that the double octave may appear, 36 to 9; and in sesquioctave, for the manifestation of the interval of a tone, 18 to 16, as was said before.

The other root mean, 2, 3, 6, has the triple ratio immediately, both in the extremes to one another and again in the differences to one another, in which ratio is the mixed concord of the octave and fifth, something that did not belong to the former mean, 3, 4, 6. And if we should also multiply the terms by themselves and into one another, and the differences by themselves and into the terms and further into one another, more ratios of concords will spring up for us, as anyone who pursues such refinements for himself can perceive. Plato’s saying too may be appropriately fitted to this mean.

For the harmonic mean is the one ‘exceeding and exceeded by the same part of the extremes themselves’, which is an attribute of no other mean: for in 2, 3, 6 the mean term exceeds and is exceeded by the same part of the extremes, that is, by a half; it exceeds the lesser and is exceeded by the greater; and in 3, 4, 6 again the mean term, by the same part of the extremes, a third, exceeds 3 and is exceeded by 6; for it does so by a unit and by a dyad. This mean was held by Pythagoras and his school to be subcontrary to the arithmetic mean, because the latter had its mean term exceeded and exceeding by a part of its own, no longer of the extremes, and by the same part; for it exceeds and is exceeded by an equal number or unit, whereas in the harmonic it is not by an equal amount. But since some wish to take this mean as subcontrary to both, the arithmetic and the geometric, whereas we said that it undergoes something subcontrary to the arithmetic alone, the following consideration too will come to our aid: for what will stand in their way is that the geometric mean is seen to undergo something mixed and to hold the position of a mean in relation to both the arithmetic and the harmonic, as to what is in each case an extreme.

For it will blend in itself the peculiar properties of each of the two. For it was peculiar to the harmonic that the mean term exceeds and is exceeded by a part of the extremes themselves which is the same in quality, even if not in quantity, but never by a part of the mean term; and to the arithmetic, conversely, that it is no longer by a part of the extremes but of the mean term, and by a part the same in quantity. In the geometric, however, the part by which the mean term exceeds and is exceeded belongs neither to the extremes alone nor to the mean term alone, but both to the mean and to the extremes; for it will exceed one of the extremes by a part of itself, and will be exceeded by the other by a part of that extreme; and the part will be the same in quality, even if not in quantity, as in the harmonic. Often, too, it will exceed and be exceeded by several parts, again the same in quality, so that it will also have something in common with the harmonic, namely that the part is the same in quality only and no longer in quantity; and in this respect the harmonic will not be subcontrary to it. Again, in the arithmetic the lesser ratios appeared among the greater terms and the greater among the lesser; in the harmonic, in the subcontrary manner, the greater among the greater and the lesser among the lesser; while in the geometric, as being in a way a mean between them, they are neither lesser nor greater, but equal.

For these reasons, then, the harmonic might reasonably be called subcontrary to the arithmetic alone, and not to the geometric as well. The harmonic has as its property that the product of the mean term and the sum of the two extremes is double the product of the extremes alone. It is generated, once more, from equality, first from units, then from dyads, then from triads and so on, by the following rules: the first term from the first and the second; the second from the first and two seconds; the third from the first, twice the second and three times the third, so that there may arise the mean which has its extremes and its differences in triple ratio. But if it is to be in double ratio: the first term from the first and twice the second; the second from twice the first and twice the second; the third from once the first, twice the second and three times the third. For from equality in units there will arise, according to the rules stated, the two root means 2, 3, 6 and 3, 4, 6; from equality in dyads their doubles, from equality in triads their triples, and so on. And upon all the formations that arise the peculiar properties of the harmonic will follow.

Just as on the canon, while the fastenings remain fixed, the movable bridge by being shifted produces a variety of concords, in the same way it is possible, when two terms are given, whether even or odd, and remain the same, to produce one mean after another, now the arithmetic, now the geometric, now that which is subcontrary to the arithmetic, that is, the harmonic.

For observe: with even terms, 40 and 10, the term 25 when made the mean produces an arithmetic mean, upon which all its peculiar properties will follow; 20 produces a geometric mean together with its peculiar properties; and 16 a harmonic mean with the attributes that belong to it. With odd terms, 45 and 5, the same 25 inserted as mean will likewise produce the arithmetic mean.

The reason is that by as much as the greater term has gained in relation to the mean, by so much has the lesser been diminished, so that the mean again exceeds and is exceeded by an equal excess; for this was the property of the arithmetic mean. And 15 inserted as mean will produce a geometric mean, and 9 the harmonic. Numbers smaller than the extremes here set out, in the odd species and in the even, which are capable of containing the three means, one would not find; these would be the root numbers and the least.

These three means alone were deemed worthy of account by the ancients, having the differences from one another and the properties in themselves that have been stated, and they were also fitted by them to the constitution and harmony of the cosmos, as we shall show elsewhere. The three that come after these were themselves also deemed worthy of acceptance from the time of Archytas and Hippasus; and the first of them, which is the fourth when it is counted together with the original three, is, as we said, called ‘subcontrary’ as its proper name, because it undergoes something subcontrary to the harmonic, on account of the ratios of the concords that have been observed in the latter. The fourth mean, then, is of this kind: of three terms, as the greater is to the lesser, so will the difference of the lesser terms be to that of the greater.

It is said to be subcontrary to the harmonic because in that mean the difference of the greater terms was the antecedent, whereas in this one it is that of the lesser. Both preserve the same extremes, both in their root forms and in the multiples of these. Examples of it will be 2, 5, 6 and 3, 5, 6; and its property is that it makes the product of the greater terms a multiple of the product of the lesser. The mean term will exceed and be exceeded neither by the same part of the extremes themselves, as in the harmonic, nor by a part of itself, as in the arithmetic, nor at once by a part of itself and of one of the extremes, as in the geometric; rather there will be a certain property peculiar to this mean in respect of the excess. This mean too is generated from equality, primarily that in units, then that in dyads and triads and so on in sequence: the first term from the first and the second; the second from the first, two seconds and two thirds; the third from once the first, twice the second and three times the third; and there will arise the mean that has its extremes in triple ratio.

In order that the one having them in double ratio may arise, one must make the first term from the first and two seconds; the second from the first, two seconds and two thirds; the third from once the first, twice the second and three times the third. The prototypes just stated, then, will arise from the equality of units, their doubles from that of dyads, their triples from that of triads, and so on in sequence. The fifth also undergoes something subcontrary, in its case to the geometric, but it is called simply ‘fifth’ because the name had already been claimed by the mean before it. It exists, then, when of three terms, as the mean is to the least, so is the difference of these same terms to that of the greater, for example 2, 4, 5. It stands in subcontrary opposition to the geometric because in that mean the difference of the greater terms was a multiple of that of the lesser, whereas in this one, conversely, that of the lesser is a multiple of that of the greater, in the same ratio, however, as that of the terms mentioned.

It has as its property that it makes the square on the mean term double the product of the least and the mean, and further the product of the greater terms double the product of the extremes. The multiples of this mean too will have the same consequences. It is generated from three equal terms: the first term from the first and the second; the mean from two firsts and two seconds; the greater from the first, two seconds and two thirds. The sixth exists when, as the greatest of the three terms is to the mean, so too is the excess of the lesser terms to that of the greater. For the same reasons as the one before it, it is opposed to the geometric; for example 1, 4, 6. Here too the difference of the lesser terms is the antecedent, whereas the geometric has as antecedent that of the greater terms; and the ratios both of the terms to one another and of the two differences to one another are sesquialter. Of the same kind too will be the ratios that render the property of this mean. For the square on the greatest term, 6, is sesquialter of the product of the greater terms, and this same product is sesquialter of the square on the mean. This mean too may be generated from three terms in equality, as follows: the first equal to the first; the second to two firsts and two seconds; the third from once the first, twice the second and three times the third.
The prototype, then, is from units, and its multiples from dyads and triads and the equalities that follow.

We have now spoken also of the three means that come next after the first ones, which were employed by those from Plato down to Eratosthenes, their discovery having been begun, as we said, by Archytas and Hippasus the mathematicians. As for the four that were ingeniously added by the more recent men who came after these, Myonides and Euphranor the Pythagoreans and their circle, it is neither right to pass them over, for that would show a want of love for what is fine, nor yet to prolong the account of them, since they possess nothing so august or so varied as those before them. We must therefore speak of them cursorily, keeping in view at the same time the due proportion of the book. We have named them simply thus: seventh, eighth, ninth and tenth.

The seventh exists when, as the greatest term is to the least, so is their difference to that of the lesser terms, for example 6, 8, 9. Its generation is from the fourth, 3, 5, 6: for adding together the extremes of that mean I set the sum as the greatest term of this one; from the least and the mean I make the mean of this one; and the greatest of that one I make the least of this. It is a consequence of this mean that the oblong contained by the greater terms has to that contained by the lesser the same ratio as the greatest term has to the least, and as the difference of the extremes has to that of the lesser terms. The eighth is observed when, as the greatest is to the least, so too is the excess of these same terms to the excess of the greatest over the mean, conversely to the one before it, for example 6, 7, 9.

The generation of this one too is from the fifth, 2, 4, 5: for adding together its greater terms I make the greatest of this one; the extremes I set as the mean of this one; and adding together in turn the lesser terms of that mean I have the lesser term of this one. It is a consequence of it that, as the greatest is to the least, so too is the product of the greater terms to the product of the lesser. The ninth exists when, as the mean term is to the least, so is the difference of the extremes to that of the lesser terms, for example 4, 6, 7.

Its peculiar property is that the product of the greater terms stands to the product of the extremes in the same ratio as the mean term to the least, and as the difference of the extremes to the difference of the lesser terms. We shall generate this one too from the sixth, 1, 4, 6: for by adding together its extremes I make the greatest term of this one, as mean I set the greatest term of that one, and as least its mean term. Thus the three means from the seventh onward will have their generations, in order, from the three before them, the fourth, the fifth and the sixth. The tenth, coming after them all, is when, as the mean term is to the lesser, so also is the difference of the extremes to the difference of the greatest from the mean, for example 3, 5, 8. The peculiar property of this one is that it is observed in superpartient ratio, and in its root form at that, but not in multiple or superparticular ratio.

And it has as a consequence that it makes the oblong contained by the lesser terms equal to that contained by the said differences; the reason is that they are the same numbers. This one too is generated from the harmonic mean 2, 3, 6, which stands before the three means just mentioned, so that consecutive means may have their generation from consecutive means, even if not from ones in regular order. Adding together, then, the extremes of that one I make the greatest term of this one; out of the lesser terms I set the mean of this one; and the mean term by itself I keep as the least of this one. Now that ten means in all have come to light for us, this too will be no ordinary encomium of the decad, bearing as it does on the fact that no perfect ratio escapes it, but that, being as it were a kind of receptacle (dechas), it receives into itself the ratios of all the things that are, and for this reason was named by the ancients All and Whole and Heaven, as we shall try to show in the account devoted to it, when, immediately after this introduction, we set out also the special properties (ἐπανθήματα) of each of the other numbers from the unit up to it.

For the present we must speak of the most perfect proportion, which exists in four terms and has been specially named musical, because the musical ratios of the concords in harmony are most clearly contained in it.

They say that it was a discovery of the Babylonians and that it first came to the Greeks through Pythagoras. Many of the Pythagoreans, at any rate, are found to have made use of it, such as Aristaeus of Croton, Timaeus of Locri, Philolaus and Archytas of Tarentum, and a good many others, and after them Plato in the Timaeus, where he speaks as follows: ‘After this he went on to fill up both the double and the triple intervals, cutting off yet further portions from that source and placing them between these, so that in each interval there were two means, the one exceeding and exceeded by the same part of the extremes themselves, the other exceeding by an equal amount in number and exceeded by an equal amount; and, sesquialter and sesquitertian intervals having arisen, he filled them up throughout with the leimma of the sesquioctave’; and so on with what follows these words, all of which will be clear after the exposition of this proportion. The proportion called musical, then, is in four terms, two extremes and two means, in such a way that the ratios of the mean terms to the extremes, being different, are interwoven in accordance with the concords that stand at their intervals in the harmonies.

For since the concords in music come about in harmony when two or even more notes not of the same pitch are blended under a single stroke and fall upon the hearing as one in form, the least and first concordant interval perceptible to the hearing is the fourth (διὰ τεσσάρων); for the strings that contain it are at that distance from one another. This is in sesquitertian ratio; and after it, when one string has been added, the whole interval is for the same reason called the fifth (διὰ πέντε), and this concord too is in a ratio, the sesquialter. The difference of the latter from the former is the interval contained by the added fifth string, which is that of a tone and is in sesquioctave ratio, so that the fifth will exceed the fourth by a tone, and the sesquialter ratio the sesquitertian by a sesquioctave. And these have been apprehended as incomposite intervals and as simple among the concords; the greater intervals compounded out of them render the concord by now more full-bodied, and first among them the so-called octave (διὰ πασῶν), which is compounded of both of those and has itself received this name because it embraces all the strings that produce the simple concords; and it is in double ratio, for the double is the combination of every sesquitertian and sesquialter ratio.

From the double itself, again, and each of the two original ones come the octave together with the fourth and the octave together with the fifth. What is called the octave together with the fourth the Pythagoreans did not think to be a concord, since it escapes multiple and superparticular ratio, and superpartient as well, and falls out into a mixed relation; for it is as 8 to 3, because 6 is the double of 3 and 8 the sesquitertian of 6. For the present, however, let it too be reckoned a concord, in accordance with the more recent writers, for the sake of clarity in what follows. After it, again, the octave together with the fifth is a concord, being in triple ratio, because the triple ratio is composed of the double and the sesquialter: for 6 is the double of 3, and 9 the sesquialter of 6, and 9 stands to 3 in triple ratio.

The double compounded with itself makes the concordant interval of the double octave, which is in quadruple ratio; for the double ratio taken twice is quadruple. The 5 concords greater than this come about when the original simple intervals are again interwoven with the double octave; these we deliberately pass over for now, since it is more opportune to give a technical account of them in the Introduction to Music itself. As for the tightenings and slackenings of the strings that take place according to the said ratios, they relate that Pythagoras was the first to measure them out: for, having gone into a smithy and caught the sound of a concordant resonance from the downward blow of the hammers, he weighed the weights against one another, and finding them * * * and in the said ratios, with great natural genius he thought the matter through and fitted the same ratios to a variety of materials, now to the lengths of strings either equal in thickness but measured against one another in respect of their shortening, or conversely equal in length but proportionally thickened, now to strings that did not differ in the aforesaid respects but were measured out differently in tension alone, and often to strings that underwent the test in respect of two or even three of the said differences.

And from there it was very easy for him to apply what is analogous to pan-pipes and auloi and wind instruments in general as well: for there too, in conformity with the stringed instruments, the lengths and the bores, when measured out according to the said ratios, produced the concords, the width and length of the pipes corresponding to thickness, length and slackness of string, and narrowness and shortness to thinness, tension and shortness. The causes on account of which this came about we shall make clear in the proper place, in the Introduction to Music itself. For the present we must consider the said ratios in numbers, as in a cursory survey. In order, then, to set off a sesquitertian ratio, one needs a number that has a third; for its sesquitertian will in every case have a half, so that the sesquialter of this latter too may be double in relation to the original number, as is the case with 6, 8, 12. Or again, in order to make a sesquialter ratio, I need a number that has a half, so that its sesquialter, when extended, necessarily having a third, may furnish a subsesquitertian ratio in relation to some other term, which will again be a multiple of the original number, as is the case with 6, 9, 12.

If, then, we keep the extreme terms fixed, since they are in fact the same in both means, I mean 6 and 12, and set the mean terms together between them, there will be the aforesaid musical proportion in four terms, 6, 8, 9, 12. We set the number 6 as its first term, since it was the first to admit of a third and a half together, in order that we might be able to set off from it the said ratios: 8 as sesquitertian, in relation to its sesquialter 12, which will be double the original 6; or again 9 as sesquialter, in relation to its sesquitertian 12, which again will be double the original number. And this is the aforementioned interweaving of the mean terms with the extremes. That it was necessary to set 6 first for the setting-off of the ratios we may learn from the following: the unit was not possible, since it is posited as partless and has neither a half nor a third; nor yet the dyad, because it has a half but has no third; nor indeed the triad, which has a third but has no half; nor the tetrad, for the same reasons as the dyad (for it too is deprived of a third); and the pentad is excluded for the same reasons as the unit, having neither a half nor a third. So 6 will be the first and least number to serve us for the settings-off of the ratios, being the product of the first two numbers that admit, the one of a half and the other of a third, I mean 2 and 3.

In relation to 6, then, 8, being its sesquitertian, will contain the concord of the fourth. And since 12 is sesquialter in relation to 8, containing the fifth, the same 12, being double in relation to the original 6, will contain the concord of the octave, which is compounded of the fourth and the fifth. And again 9, being the sesquialter of 6, will contain the fifth, and 12 in relation to 9 the fourth, being its sesquitertian, and in relation to the original 6 once more the octave. The excess of the fifth over the fourth, the interval of a tone, will be contained by the mean terms, 9 in relation to 8, which are in sesquioctave ratio, because the sesquialter ratio exceeds the sesquitertian by a sesquioctave, as has been said. Moreover the difference of the greater terms, 12 and 9, in relation to that of 8 and 6 will contain the sesquialter ratio, which belongs to the concord of the fifth; and, by interweaving, the difference of 12 and 8 in relation to the difference of 9 and 6 will have the sesquitertian ratio of the concord of the fourth; and the double ratio will be had by the difference of 8 and 6 in relation to the difference of 8 and 9, and by the difference of 12 and 8 in relation to the difference of 8 and 6, and further by the difference of 12 and 6 in relation to the difference of 9 and 6; for in each pairing the double is the ratio of the concord of the octave.

The triple ratio, for the concord of the octave and fifth, will be contained by the difference of 9 and 6 in relation to the difference of 9 and 8, or also by the difference of 12 and 6 in relation to the difference of 8 and 6. And the quadruple ratio, that of the concord of the double octave, by the difference of 12 and 8 in relation to the difference of 9 and 8. One might find still more ratios of the concordant intervals by multiplying the four terms set out, each by itself and by one another, and further by their differences, and the differences themselves both by themselves and by one another, as each person can come to see by trying it for himself, out of love of what is fine. Once again, then, there is a musical mean when, in four terms, as the greatest is to the one next to it, so the lesser of the mean terms is to the least; and as the greatest is to the lesser of the mean terms, so the greater of the mean terms is to the least. It has as a consequence that it makes the oblong contained by the extremes equal to the heteromecic number produced by the mean terms. And it alone contains the three primary means as well: the arithmetic mean in the terms 12, 9, 6, for the mean term exceeds and is exceeded by an equal amount; the harmonic in the terms 12, 8, 6, for the mean term exceeds and is exceeded by the same part of the extremes themselves; and the geometric in disjunction, for as 12 is to 8, so is 9 to 6, so that the sameness of the ratios is rendered through the 4 terms.

Let this, for the present, be the end of our Introduction according to Nicomachus the Pythagorean; on another occasion, god granting, we shall compose and provide for you this same Introduction to Arithmetic itself in more complete form, as for one who has by then acquired through the present one a disposition capable of following it; and all the other things that flower upon the numbers from the unit to the decad, according to the physical account and the ethical and, prior even to these, the theological, we shall set in order and study together with you, so that from them the exposition of the three introductions that come next, I mean the musical, the geometrical and the spherical, may thereafter become easier and most ready for you.
